title: How to hold the yarn
subtitle: Controlling tension through your hand so stitches come out consistent
excerpt: The working yarn feeds through your fingers onto the hook. How you hold it determines how much tension it carries. Find a hold that is consistent and comfortable.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: The length of yarn attached to the ball or skein that you actively use to form stitches, as distinct from yarn tails or already-worked sections.
The amount of resistance in the working yarn as it feeds onto the hook. Consistent tension produces stitches of uniform size.

content.text: The way you hold the
working yarn
determines how much resistance it has as it feeds through your fingers onto the hook. A consistent hold produces even
yarn tension
. A grip that tightens and loosens produces stitches that vary in size.
Two common holds
There is no single correct way to hold yarn. Two holds are widely used:

Index finger hold: drape the working yarn over your index finger, weave it under the middle finger, over the ring finger, and hold the tail against your palm with the little finger. The index finger rises slightly to feed yarn onto the hook, then lowers to let it pass.

Wrapped index hold: wrap the working yarn once or twice around the index finger and hold the remaining yarn loosely against the palm. The wrap provides friction that replaces the weave in the first method.
Try both. The one that produces the most consistent stitches for you is the right one. Neither is inherently better.
Holding the work

Your non-hook hand also holds the work itself. Pinch the fabric just below the active stitch with your thumb and middle finger. This gives the hook something to pull against when drawing up loops. As you work along the row, move the pinch forward every few stitches so it stays just below the hook.
Finding comfortable tension
Work a small swatch of ten stitches over five rows. Do not worry about pattern or gauge at this stage.
After each row, hold the swatch flat and check that the stitches look roughly the same size from left to right.
If stitches are small and tight, ease the grip or let more yarn over the finger. If stitches are large and loose, increase the wrap or tension the yarn against more fingers.
Keep adjusting until the hook enters each stitch without pulling hard and without falling through loosely.
Common problems

items.symptom: Stitches are tight and hard to enter with the hook
items.cause: The yarn is gripped too firmly or wrapped too many times.
items.fix: Reduce the number of wraps around the finger, or hold the yarn over fewer fingers so it can feed more freely.

items.cause: There is not enough friction in the yarn hold.
items.fix: Add one more finger to the weave, or wrap the yarn one extra time around the index finger to create more resistance.

items.cause: The grip on both the hook and the yarn is too tight.
items.fix: Set the work down, shake out the hand, and restart with a deliberate light grip. Tension comes from the yarn path, not from squeezing.

content.text: What to try next

Once a comfortable hold is established, work a tension swatch for the pattern you want to make and measure it against the stated gauge. If the gauge is off, try adjusting the hold slightly before changing hook size. See the gauge guide for details.
